slides.title: Introduction to IP Addressing

slides.title: IP Address Assignment
slides.body:
Where Do IP Addresses Come From?
An IP address is a unique logical address assigned to every device on a network

slides.title: IP Address Assignment
slides.body:
Where Do IP Addresses Come From?
Every device on a network needs an IP address to communicate. IP addresses can be classified based on how they are assigned to a device – either manually (Static) or automatically (Dynamic)

slides.title: IP Address Assignment
slides.body:
Where Do IP Addresses Come From?
Static IP
Manually configured by an administrator, Fixed, and Never changes
Dynamic IP
Automatically assigned by a DHCP server from a pool of available addresses when a device joins the network

slides.title: IP Address Assignment
slides.body:
Dynamic IP
Assigned for a limited time (lease) and may change
Used for laptops, phones, and user devices
Automatically assigned by a DHCP server
Static IP
Remains fixed unless manually changed
Used for servers, routers, printers
Manually configured by an administrator
Basis

slides.title: DHCP - Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
slides.body:
Definition
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is an Application Layer protocol that automatically assigns IP configuration information to devices on a network

slides.title: DHCP - Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
slides.body:
What DHCP provides to a device?
IP Address
Logical address used to identify the device on the network
Subnet Mask
Defines the network and host portions of the IP address
Default Gateway
The router’s IP address used to send traffic to other networks
DNS Server Address
Translates domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses
Lease Duration
The time period for which the device is allowed to use the assigned IP address

slides.title: DHCP - Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
slides.body:
Key Technical Points
Uses UDP - Port 67 (server), Port 68 (client)
Runs at the Application Layer

slides.title: DHCP - Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
slides.body:
Key Technical Points
DHCP follows a client–server model where the DHCP server manages a pool of IP addresses and assigns them to clients
Uses UDP instead of TCP because the client initially does not know its IP address and must send broadcast messages to discover a DHCP server

slides.title: DHCP — The DORA Process
slides.body:
Four Steps to Get an IP Address
When a device joins a network and needs an IP address, DHCP follows a four-step process called DORA

slides.title: DHCP — The DORA Process
slides.body:
1
DHCP Discover (Client → Broadcast)
Device has no IP yet. It shouts to the entire network: "Is there a DHCP server here?"
Source IP: 0.0.0.0   |   Destination: 255.255.255.255 (broadcast)
Carries the client's MAC address so the server can identify it
Four Steps to Get an IP Address

slides.title: DHCP — The DORA Process
slides.body:
2
DHCP Offer (Server → Client)
DHCP server replies with an available IP address and full configuration
If multiple servers exist, all of them send an Offer - the client picks the first one received
Four Steps to Get an IP Address

slides.title: DHCP — The DORA Process
slides.body:
3
DHCP Request (Client → Broadcast)
Client accepts one offer and broadcasts its selection so all other DHCP servers know their offers were not chosen and can return those IP addresses to the pool
Four Steps to Get an IP Address

slides.title: DHCP — The DORA Process
slides.body:
4
DHCP Acknowledge (Server → Client)
The selected DHCP server sends a DHCPACK confirming the assignment. The device configures its network interface and the lease period begins
Four Steps to Get an IP Address

slides.title: DHCP Lease
slides.body:
IP Addresses Are Borrowed, Not Owned
A DHCP lease is a time-limited assignment of an IP address. The device uses the IP only for the lease duration - after that, it must renew or lose the address

slides.title: DHCP Lease
slides.body:
IP Addresses Are Borrowed, Not Owned
Devices join and leave networks constantly. Leases ensure IP addresses are returned to the pool and reused

slides.title: DHCP Lease
slides.body:
Renewal - Two Timers
Client sends a DHCPREQUEST message (unicast) to the same DHCP server
T1 (50% of lease time)
If T1 failed, client broadcasts a Request to any available DHCP server
T2 (87.5% of lease time)
If both T1 and T2 failed, the device loses its IP and restarts the full DORA process
Expiry (100%)

slides.title: DHCP Lease
slides.body:
Renewal - Two Timers
DHCP Release
A device can voluntarily return its IP before expiry by sending a DHCPRELEASE message - this happens when a device gracefully disconnects

slides.title: DHCP Lease
slides.body:
Analogy
Returning early = DHCP Release

slides.body:

slides.title: DHCP Relay Agent
slides.body:

The Solution - DHCP Relay Agent

slides.title: DHCP Relay Agent
slides.body:
One DHCP Server for Multiple Networks
Client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER on its local subnet
Relay Agent (router) intercepts the broadcast
Relay Agent forwards it as a unicast to the DHCP server's IP address.(Configured using ip helper-address command on the router.)

slides.title: DHCP Relay Agent
slides.body:
One DHCP Server for Multiple Networks
DHCP server processes it and sends the Offer back to the Relay Agent
Relay Agent forwards the Offer to the client
This allows one centralized DHCP server to serve multiple subnets
Without a relay agent, every subnet would need its own DHCP server

slides.title: How ARP Works
slides.body:
Broadcast Request, Unicast Reply
1
ARP Request (Broadcast):
Device A sends an ARP Request as a broadcast on the local subnet
Destination MAC: FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF (broadcast — all devices receive it)
Message: "Who has IP 192.168.1.20? Please tell me your MAC address."
All devices receive this. Each one checks: "Is this my IP?" Only the matching device responds

slides.title: How ARP Works
slides.body:
Broadcast Request, Unicast Reply
2
ARP Reply (Unicast):
Device B (owner of 192.168.1.20) replies directly to Device A
Reply: "My IP is 192.168.1.20 and my MAC is 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E."
Device A now has the MAC address and can deliver the data

slides.title: ARP Cache
slides.body:
Temporary Storage of IP–MAC Mappings
Every device maintains an ARP Cache - a table that maps IP addresses to MAC addresses learned through ARP
After receiving an ARP Reply, the device stores the IP-MAC mapping in its cache
Next time the same IP is needed, the device checks the cache first - no broadcast needed

slides.body:

slides.title: RARP - Reverse ARP
slides.body:
MAC to IP Mapping
A diskless device boots and knows only its MAC address
It broadcasts: "My MAC is 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. What IP should I use?"
Sends a RARP Broadcast Request
A RARP Server looks up the MAC in its table and replies with the assigned IP address
The device configures its network interface using that IP

slides.title: RARP - Reverse ARP
slides.body:
MAC to IP Mapping
RARP could provide only an IP address
Required a RARP server on every subnet (no relay support)
Replaced by BOOTP (1985), then replaced again by DHCP (1993)
DHCP handles all of RARP's use cases and much more - RARP is now only of historical interest
